cards.title: THE FAMILY ROOM
cards.tagline: SIX ZONES. START WHERE THE CABLES CROSS THE FLOOR.
cards.objective: The family room carries more jobs than any other room in the house: screens, floor play, games, blankets, charging, and craft all compete for the same square meters. This card is the map.
zones_in_order: FRZ-003 Board Game and Puzzle Zone
cards.start_here: FRZ-001 Primary Media Zone. Run the Primary Media Zone first. Its cables cross the floor into the other zones, and its cabinet is where stray controllers, chargers, and disc cases quietly collect, so clearing it lets the other five zones tell you the truth about themselves.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the six ZONE cards face up. Pick the one that is annoying you today, or take the one this card says to start at.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your family room. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 6. With more than one, deal the friction cards out and let each person keep the ones they believe. Disagreement is the useful part, not a problem to resolve before starting.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do FRA-013 The Full Family Room Hazard Walk before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers the television's anti-tip strap, the vent heat behind the media unit, the cables crossing the floor, the charging station's cable loop, and the hot glue gun on the craft table.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A flat screen on a low unit tips forward when a child pulls on the frame or climbs the shelf underneath it. Check the strap or the mount bolts with your hand, not your eye.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Consoles and streaming boxes vent through slots on the top and back. A blanket laid over one, a stack of disc cases on top, or a cabinet door kept shut during play traps that heat against the board.

the_call.title: The console with the save files
the_call.text: You are keeping a previous-generation console because someone's save file lives on it, and that is a genuine reason. It is also exactly why it has sat unplugged behind the newer machine for two years. Settle it in this session rather than the next one. Plug it in now, and either move the save data to a card or to the current console, or hand a controller to the child and sit through one real session to find out whether anyone still cares. If it will not power on, or nobody asks for it again after that evening, you are storing a box of plastic guarding a memory it can no longer play. Photograph the save screen if it matters to someone, then route the console, its controllers, and its cables out together in one trip. Splitting them up is how half of it ends up back in the cabinet.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush

the_call.title: The gift nobody plays with
the_call.text: There is a large, loud, expensive thing in this room that a relative gave, and no child has chosen it unprompted in months. You keep it because of the giver, and every time you sort this zone you move it two feet and put it back. The rule that settles this: the shelf belongs to the child, not to the giver. Run one honest week, touch nothing, and watch whether any child reaches for it without being pointed at it. If none does, it goes. If you are genuinely worried about being asked, take one photograph of the child playing with it, send that photo to the person who gave it, then donate it while the good will is intact. Keeping an unloved toy on the lowest shelf does not honour anybody. It costs a bin that a favourite toy currently does not have.

the_call.title: The game with one piece missing
the_call.text: This is the decision the shelf has been avoiding for years, and the answer is not the same for every box. Split missing pieces into two kinds. Substitutable: a lost meeple, a token, a die, a bill of play money. Those you can replace with a coin, a button, a printed sheet, or a request to the publisher. Structural: a lost rules booklet, a board section, a card from a deck that must be complete, or a single puzzle piece. Those cannot be substituted, and the game is over no matter how good the box looks on the shelf. Here is the mechanism that makes it stick. Write the missing item and today's date on a sticky note and stick it to the lid. Any box still wearing that note when you next reset this shelf leaves the house. That turns a vague guilt you have carried for years into a deadline you can either meet or honestly fail.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A fleece throw laid over a radiator, a portable heater, or a lamp shade to dry or to be out of the way. Synthetic fabric against a hot surface is a slow fire that starts once the room is empty.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: A throw that slides off the sofa arm onto the floor beside it lands exactly where the next person puts their foot when they stand up in the dark.

the_call.title: The ugly favourite
the_call.text: You own a pilled grey fleece that everyone in the house fights over, and a handsome wool throw that has been folded on the arm of the chair since the day it was bought. The instinct is to keep the wool one because it looks like the room you want, and quietly retire the fleece because it looks tired. Do the opposite, and be clear about why: this basket stores comfort, not decoration. The test is reaches, not looks. Watch a week and count which throws come off the pile. The tired fleece stays, because it is doing the job the basket exists for. The wool one goes to the guest bed, where being beautiful and unused is actually the job, or it goes out. The same rule handles the blanket a relative knitted. If someone genuinely wraps up in it, it stays in the basket. If it is an heirloom nobody unfolds, it does not belong in a family room basket at all. Fold it into the linen closet, or give it to the person in the family who will actually use it.

cards.done_looks_like: One power strip on a hard surface, four or five labeled cables each ending at a named slot, the empty slots visible during the day, and no charger plugged into any other socket in the room.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A tablet or battery pack charging on a cushion, under a blanket, or inside a closed bin. Any pack that is swollen, hot to hold, or bulging at the seam comes off the strip immediately and does not go back on.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: A charging cable long enough to hang from the side table down to the floor makes a loop at exactly a toddler's neck height. Shorten it or clip it flat to the surface.

the_call.title: The old phone with the photos on it
the_call.text: The cable drawer is the easy half of this zone, and you already know the answer: match every cable to a live device, keep one spare of each connector type in a labeled bag, recycle the rest. The hard part is the drawer's other resident, the retired phone. You have kept it for two reasons that quietly contradict each other, as a backup in case something breaks, and as an archive because there are photos on it you have never transferred. It cannot serve both, and right now it is serving neither. Settle it here. A backup phone is one you have charged and switched on within the last year, and if you have not, it will be flat and out of date on the day you need it. An archive is one you transfer today, in this session, while the device is in your hand and the charger is right there. Do the transfer now, or say out loud that you never will, and then recycle the handset with the battery still in it at a proper collection point rather than leaving it in a drawer to swell.

safety_checks.text: A glue gun left plugged in on the table after everyone walks away. The tip holds enough heat to burn a hand or scorch the surface long after the last bead of glue.

the_call.title: The half-finished project
the_call.text: There is a bag or a box here holding something started with real enthusiasm and abandoned somewhere in the middle, and it has held the good end of the work surface for months. The problem is that clearing it feels like quitting, so it stays and nothing else gets started. Use this test, out loud, project by project. Name the very next physical action and name the day you will do it. Not the goal, the action. Cut the second sleeve. Buy the size four needles. If you cannot produce both halves without stalling, the project is finished, and it finished a while ago without telling you. Break it down. The good materials go back into the paper, drawing, and glue bins where the next project can use them. The partly worked piece goes to somebody who will finish it, or it goes out. And you get back the one thing this zone is actually short of, which is a clear surface for the project that has enthusiasm behind it right now.

steps: Pull every disc case, spare remote, headset, and loose cable out of the cabinet onto the floor. Anything that pairs with a console or a television you no longer own leaves today, including any remote you have been keeping in case. Label both ends of every remaining cable and tape a pairing card inside the cabinet door naming which controller and headset belong to which console.

steps: Pull every toy off the shelf and run the two-question sort in the open: does a child actually reach for this without being pointed at it, and is it in one piece with no small part loose enough to choke on. Anything nobody has chosen in the last honest week, and anything cracked or missing a piece that could be swallowed, comes off the shelf today.
Sort what remains into five or six open bins, one category each.

cards.title: COUNT EVERY BOX AND STICKY-NOTE WHAT'S MISSING
cards.objective: Check each box's piece count and label the ones that are missing something with a date.
cards.why_it_matters: A box that looks complete on the shelf and empties out short at game night is worse than an empty shelf, because it wastes the one evening you had to play it.
steps: Pull every box and check its lid for a name label and a tape strip on the short edge. While each one is open, count the pieces against the box's own list. If something is missing, decide now whether it's substitutable (a token, a die, a bill of play money you can replace) or structural (a rules booklet, a board section, a single puzzle piece). Write the missing item and today's date on a sticky note on any box you are not fixing immediately.
Stack the checked boxes no more than five high, name readable on the short edge.
cards.victory_condition: Every box on the shelf is labeled and stacked no more than five high, and any box missing a piece carries a dated sticky note naming exactly what is gone.

cards.title: SETTLE EVERY DATED STICKY NOTE AND RESTACK BY REACH
cards.objective: Decide substitutable or structural for every box still carrying a dated missing-piece note, act on it, and restack so the bottom of any deep pile is not the one played most.
cards.why_it_matters: A vague guilt about an incomplete game turns into a deadline you can meet or honestly fail the moment it is written down and dated, and a stack that always makes you move five boxes to reach the one you want is charging you rent every game night.
steps: Pull every box still wearing a dated sticky note.
For a substitutable loss, replace it now with a coin, button, printed sheet, or a request to the publisher, and remove the note.
For a structural loss, or any note still on a box from before today, take the game off the shelf and donate or recycle it.
Restack so the games played most often sit on top or at a reachable height, not buried under five others.
cards.victory_condition: No box on the shelf carries a sticky note older than today, every remaining box has passed its count, and the games played most are not buried at the bottom of a stack.

cards.title: FOLD, TEST BY REACHES, AND RELOCATE THE DECORATIVE ONE
cards.objective: Fold every throw to match, test the basket by what people actually reach for, and give the decorative one a real home elsewhere.
cards.why_it_matters: The test is reaches, not looks: a basket that stores comfort has to hold what people actually pull off the pile.
inputs: a laundry basket for anything leaving
the guest room as a destination
steps: Pull every throw and cushion out and fold each throw to the same rectangle so the fold edges line up in the basket. Run the reaches test out loud: which ones actually get pulled off the pile in an average week. The decorative one nobody reaches for goes to the guest bed or out, and a genuine heirloom nobody unfolds goes to the linen closet or to the person who will actually use it.
cards.victory_condition: One basket holds one throw per regular seat plus one spare, all folded to the same rectangle, and nothing is draped over the sofa back, a radiator, or a chair arm.

cards.title: MOVE EVERY THROW OFF THE RADIATOR AND SHORTEN THE NIGHT ROUTINE
cards.objective: Clear every throw off the radiator, heater, or lamp shade for good, and agree the last-lamp fold-back routine.
cards.why_it_matters: Synthetic fabric left against a hot surface once the room empties is a slow fire that starts after everyone has gone to bed.
steps: Walk the room and move every throw draped over a radiator, heater, or lamp shade back into the basket.
Agree out loud: when the last lamp goes off, whoever is last up folds any throw back into the basket before leaving the room.
Check that the basket itself is not blocking the walked path between the sofa and the door.
cards.victory_condition: No throw is draped over a radiator, heater, or lamp shade anywhere in the room, and the last-lamp fold-back routine is agreed out loud.

cards.title: MATCH EVERY CABLE AND SETTLE THE OLD PHONE
cards.objective: Match every cable to a device the house uses, stock one spare connector of each type, and settle the retired phone for good.
cards.why_it_matters: A retired phone serving as both an unused backup and a never-made archive is doing neither job while it takes up the drawer, and a full strip cluttered with dead connections is why the next device ends up charging somewhere unsafe.
inputs: a labeled bag for spare connectors
steps: Match every cable at the station to a device the house actually uses, and keep one spare of each connector type in a labeled bag. Pull the retired phone out of the drawer, charge it, and decide out loud whether it is genuinely a backup or an archive. If it is an archive, transfer the photos now while it is charged and in your hand; if it is neither, recycle it with the battery still in it at a proper collection point.
cards.victory_condition: Every cable at the station ends at a named device the house uses, the retired phone has been settled as backup, archive, or recycled, and no charger is plugged in anywhere else in the room.

cards.title: NAME THE NEXT ACTION OR BREAK DOWN THE PROJECT
cards.objective: Name the very next physical action and the day for any project on the table, or break it down for good.
cards.why_it_matters: A project that cannot produce a next action and a day finished a while ago without telling anyone, and it is the only thing standing between this table and dinner.
inputs: a bag for a partly worked piece leaving the house
steps: For any project sitting on the work surface, name its very next physical action and the day you will do it, out loud. If you can't produce both without stalling, the project is finished whether it says so or not. Break it down: good materials go back into the paper, drawing, or glue bins where the next project can use them, and the partly worked piece goes to someone who will finish it or goes out. Put the scissors point down in the cup and unplug the glue gun.
cards.victory_condition: The work surface is completely clear except for at most one active project bin, every scissors sits point down in its cup, and the glue gun is unplugged.

cards.title: UNPLUG THE GLUE GUN, POINT THE SCISSORS DOWN, AND SHELVE THE SMALL PARTS
cards.objective: Set a hard stop for hot tools and small parts every time the table is used: scissors point down, glue gun unplugged, beads and solvents up high.
cards.why_it_matters: A hot glue tip and blade-up scissors within a child's reach, and beads on a floor shared with a crawling child, are safety constraints that outrank how the table looks.
inputs: a high shelf for beads, solvents, and craft knives
steps: Move all seed beads, googly eyes, pompoms, and solvent-based markers to a shelf above the youngest child's reach.

Agree that the glue gun gets unplugged the moment nobody is actively using it, not at the end of the session.
cards.victory_condition: Beads, solvents, and craft knives sit above the youngest child's reach, scissors stand point down in the cup, and the glue gun is unplugged whenever it is not in use.
